newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Council set to seal mandate for air talks with E.Europe.
newsitem.headline: Council set to seal mandate for air talks with E.Europe.

text.p: The Transport Council is due on Thursday to agree a mandate for the European Commission to begin air liberalisation talks which could lead to a 25-country single market for aviation.

The negotiations, which could begin as early as January next year if the mandate goes through, would be a step towards replacement of the current spider's web of bilateral agreements across the region.
"What we could do, little by little, is to unravel that complicated web and replace it with a more straightforward relationship," a Commission official told Reuters.
Eventual talks would involve the EU and 10 countries, namely Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia.
Chances for a deal look bright, according to an Irish presidency diplomat.
"I think there's very broad agreement as to what the final mandate should look like," the diplomat told reporters ahead of Thursday's meeting in Luxembourg.

The mandate would represent a balance between gradual liberalisation of air traffic rights in the region and the need for increased harmonisation of safety and technical rules in the former Warsaw Pact countries, the diplomat said.
Agreement is likely to be far less controversial than a separate negotiating mandate, which ministers adopted in June, for bilateral "open skies" talks between the EU and Washington.
"The context is quite different," the diplomat said, adding that the central and east Europeans were set on eventually joining the EU.
"We are talking about countries adopting (EU) legislation, we know what our final objectives are. What we are talking about is very clear," he said.
"In the case of the U.S., there is a much different context. Both sides have to work out what are their long-term objectives," he added.
It is difficult to say how long talks will last or whether some countries will move ahead of others in their dealings with Brussels, the Commission official said.
"The first meeting would be mainly a contact with all those countries, preferably all together, and then we will see whether we can keep them together.

"I do not think any of those countries would be in a position to accept open access right away. Perhaps also their technical standards are not really up to those which we have in the (EU)," the official said.
